title: Senior's toolkit: data and networks
summary: Volumes, mounts, user-defined networks and the commands that show where data lives and who can reach whom.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: data and networks
steps.body: "Where did my data go?" and "why can't the api reach the database?" are the two classic container tickets. These commands answer both.

toolkit.cmd: docker volume ls / docker volume inspect <name>
toolkit.what: Lists named volumes and shows where one lives on the host and who created it.
flags: mountpoint, driver and labels (compose adds its project name)

toolkit.what: Mounts a host folder with explicit, readable options. Unlike `-v`, it fails if the source path does not exist instead of creating an empty folder.
flags: named volume, host folder, or memory only
the container cannot write to it
the short form for the same thing

toolkit.what: Shows what is really mounted where. Reveals a typo that wrote data into an anonymous volume.
A user-defined network gives containers DNS by name. The default bridge does not.
toolkit.example: docker network create shop && docker run -d --name db --network shop -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=dev postgres:17

toolkit.what: Lists the containers on a network with their IPs. If the api is not in the list, it cannot resolve the database.
Joins a debugging container to another container's network namespace, with dig, curl, ss and tcpdump ready to use.
flags: share the api's network stack, including its localhost
join the network as a new member
toolkit.example: docker run --rm -it --network container:api nicolaka/netshoot dig +short db
toolkit.when: the app image has no shell or tools

toolkit.what: Backs up a named volume to a tar file on the host, with a throwaway container.
toolkit.example: docker run --rm -v shop_pgdata:/data -v "$PWD":/backup alpine tar czf /backup/pgdata.tgz -C /data .

steps.prompt: The api container logs `Connection refused (localhost:5432)`. Postgres runs in another container called `db` on the same user-defined network. What do you change?
options: The connection string host: `Host=db` instead of `localhost`
steps.explain: Inside a container, `localhost` is that container itself. Containers on the same user-defined network reach each other by name. Publishing ports is only for the host and the outside world.

steps.prompt: After `docker rm -f db` and starting it again, Postgres is empty. It was started with `-v /var/lib/postgresql/data`. Why?
options: That made an anonymous volume; the new container got a fresh one. Use a named volume: `-v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data`
Postgres deletes its data on restart
Volumes are always deleted with the container
steps.explain: `-v /path` with no name creates an anonymous volume tied to that one container. A named volume survives and is reused. `docker inspect -f '{{json .Mounts}}'` shows which kind you have.

steps.prompt: Match the mount to what it is for.
pairs: database files that must survive the container
config from the host the app may not change
scratch space in memory, gone on stop

steps.prompt: Create a network and start Postgres on it with a named volume.
code: docker run -d --name db --__2__ shop -v __3__:/var/lib/postgresql/data -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=dev postgres:17
steps.explain: `network create` makes it, `--network` attaches the container, and a name before the colon makes a named volume. `--link` is legacy; user-defined networks replace it.

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Name every volume that holds state, and back it up with a throwaway container before any risky change. When a container cannot reach another, check `docker network inspect` and the host name in the connection string before anything else.
